fields.title: Tell Me the Story – Book 1: In the Beginning
fields.subtitle: Old Testament Stories from Genesis
fields.description: Twenty-one Bible stories from Genesis for children aged 6 to 10, each short enough to read aloud at bedtime: God making the world, the snake's trick, Noah and the rainbow, Abraham counting the stars, Jacob's stairway to heaven, and Joseph from his colourful robe to “I am Joseph!” Every story ends with a prayer and three questions to talk about together. The first book of Tell Me the Story.
fields.about_html:
Tell Me the Story is an original Ochorus storybook Bible for children aged 6 to 10, in eight books and three parts: Old Testament Stories, The Life of Jesus, and New Testament Stories. Its name comes from Katherine Hankey’s hymn “Tell Me the Old, Old Story”. God is the hero of every story, and the whole Bible is one story that leads to Jesus.

Book 1, “In the Beginning”, tells twenty-one stories from Genesis, from creation to Joseph forgiving his brothers. Each takes about four minutes to read aloud. It opens with a verse from the Bible and ends with a short prayer. Where the New Testament itself links a story to Jesus, as John 1:51 does with Jacob’s stairway, a line says so.

The stories stay close to what the Bible says, and the people in them say what the Bible says they said, in simple words. Hard stories, like Cain and Abel, the flood and Abraham on the mountain, are told honestly but gently. Under each story are three questions to talk about together, with answers for the grown-up reading along, and the passage to find in your own Bible.

qa.question: What is Tell Me the Story?
qa.answer: A storybook Bible for children aged 6 to 10, in eight books: three of Old Testament Stories, three on the life of Jesus, and two of New Testament Stories. Each story is short enough to read aloud at bedtime and ends with a prayer and three questions to talk about together.

qa.question: Which stories are in Book 1?
qa.answer: Twenty-one stories from Genesis: creation, the garden, the snake's trick, Cain and Abel, Noah, the rainbow, the tower of Babel, Abram setting out, counting the stars, Sarah laughing, Hagar and the God who sees, Abraham on the mountain, Rebekah at the well, Jacob and Esau, Jacob's stairway, Jacob wrestling, and five stories of Joseph.

qa.question: Does it change what the Bible says?
qa.answer: No. The stories are retold in simple words, but they add no events, characters or speeches the Bible doesn't give. Every verse quoted with its reference is word for word from the Berean Standard Bible.

qa.question: Are the hard stories suitable for young children?
qa.answer: They are told honestly but gently, without frightening detail. Cain and Abel, the flood and Abraham on the mountain are each told in a sentence or two, and then the story turns to what God did. The questions help a grown-up talk them through.

qa.question: How does it point to Jesus?
qa.answer: Where the New Testament itself links an Old Testament story to Jesus, such as Jacob's stairway (John 1:51) or the lamb God provided (John 1:29), the story ends with a short "Looking ahead to Jesus" line. Where the New Testament makes no link, the story doesn't force one.

qa.question: Can it be read aloud?
qa.answer: Yes, that is what it is written for. Each story takes about four minutes to read aloud. Each chapter also has a Listen button that reads the story at a gentle speed and then asks the three questions.

fields.title: Introduction: The Best Story of All
fields.body_html:
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” — Genesis 1:1

Do you like stories? Stories about brave people, and long journeys, and big surprises? This book is full of them. But these stories are special, because they are true. They come from the Bible, the book God gave us so that we could know Him.

The Bible is really one long story, the best story of all. It begins with God making the world and everything in it. Then something goes badly wrong, and the rest of the story is about how God sets out to put it right. He makes promises, and He keeps every one of them. And all the way through, the story is getting ready for someone very important: God’s own Son, Jesus.

This first book tells the stories from Genesis, the very first book of the Bible. You will meet Adam and Eve, Noah and his great boat, Abraham who looked up at the stars, and Joseph with his colourful robe. Some of them were brave and some of them were not. Some of them did terrible things. But in every story God is there, keeping His promises and taking care of His people.

Each story begins with a verse from the Bible and ends with a prayer. After the prayer there are some questions to talk about with the grown-up who is reading with you. If you want, you can find the story in your own Bible too, and read it there.

So snuggle up, and let’s begin at the very beginning.

For grown-ups: Each story takes about four minutes to read aloud. The stories stay close to what the Bible says, and the people in them say what the Bible says they said, in simple words. Hard stories, like the flood and Joseph’s brothers, are told honestly but gently. Under each story are three questions with answers to help you talk together. The first two go back over the story, and the third brings it home.

Dear God, thank you for the Bible and for all its true stories. As we read them, help us to know you and to love you. Amen.

study_questions.question: Where do the stories in this book come from?
study_questions.answer: From the Bible, the book God gave us so that we could know Him. That means they are true stories, not made-up ones.

study_questions.question: What is the Bible’s one big story about?
study_questions.answer: God made a good world, something went badly wrong, and God set out to put it right, keeping every promise He made. The whole story leads to Jesus.

study_questions.question: Which Bible story do you already know? Which one are you looking forward to?
study_questions.answer: Any answer is a good one. If your child knows a story already, let them tell it to you in their own words.

fields.title: God Makes Everything
fields.body_html:
“And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good.” — Genesis 1:31

Long, long ago, before there were any people or animals or trees, before there was even a sky or a sun, there was God. God has always been there. He never had a beginning, and He will never have an end.

In the beginning there was no world at all, only deep, dark water, and everything was empty. But God was there, and God spoke.

“Let there be light,” God said, and there was light! God saw that the light was good. He called the light “day” and the darkness “night”. That was the first day.

On the second day God made the sky, high above the waters, like a great blue roof.

On the third day God gathered the waters together into seas, and dry land appeared. Then God said, “Let the land grow plants,” and all at once the earth was green. There was grass and there were flowers, and trees heavy with apples and figs and every kind of fruit.

On the fourth day God made the lights in the sky: the bright, hot sun to rule the day, and the soft, silver moon to rule the night. And He made the stars too, so many that no one could ever count them.

On the fifth day God filled the seas with swimming creatures: tiny fish and enormous whales, wriggly ones and spotty ones. And He filled the sky with birds that flapped and swooped and sang.

On the sixth day God made the animals that live on the land: lions and lambs, elephants and ants, cows and kangaroos and creepy-crawly beetles.

Then God made something even more special. He made people. “So God created man in His own image” (Genesis 1:27). That means people are like God in a special way. We can think and love and talk with Him. God made a man and a woman, and He blessed them, and gave them the whole wonderful world to look after.

God looked at everything He had made: the light and the sky, the seas and the land, the plants and the stars, the fish and the birds and the animals and the people. And it was very, very good.

On the seventh day God rested. He wasn’t tired, because God never gets tired. He rested because His work was finished, and He made the seventh day a special day of rest.

Everything you can see, the sun that wakes you up, the trees and the rain, the dog next door and the stars at night, God made it all. And He made you too.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible tells us that God’s Son, Jesus, was there at the very beginning. “Through Him all things were made” (John 1:3). The One who made the stars would one day come to live on the earth He had made.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 1:1–2:3

Dear God, thank you for making the whole world, and for making me. Thank you that everything you make is good. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did God make on the first day, and what did He make on the sixth day?
study_questions.answer: On the first day God made light. On the sixth day He made the animals that live on the land, and then the first man and woman.

study_questions.question: What did God think of everything He had made?
study_questions.answer: He saw that it was very good. Nothing was broken or spoiled.

study_questions.question: What is your favourite thing that God made? Why?
study_questions.answer: Any answer is a good one. You could thank God for that thing together, because everything good in the world comes from Him.

fields.title: A Garden for Adam and Eve
fields.body_html:
“Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.” — Genesis 2:15

The Bible tells us more about how God made the first man. God took some dust from the ground and shaped a man out of it. Then God breathed into him the breath of life, and the man opened his eyes and was alive! His name was Adam.

God planted a beautiful garden in a place called Eden. It was full of trees that were lovely to look at and good to eat from. A river flowed through the garden to water it. And in the middle of the garden there were two special trees: the tree of life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

God put Adam in the garden to work in it and take care of it. Adam could pick fruit from every tree he liked. There was only one rule.

“You may eat from any tree in the garden,” God told him, “but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. If you eat from it, you will die.”

It was a very good rule, and an easy one to keep. The garden was full of good things, and only one tree was not for Adam.

Then God brought all the animals to Adam, to see what he would call them. Adam looked at each one and gave it a name. Perhaps he looked at the giraffe and the hippo and the hedgehog. Whatever Adam called each animal, that was its name.

But even with all those animals, there was no one quite like Adam, no one to be his friend and helper. God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

So God made Adam fall into a deep sleep. While he slept, God took one of Adam’s ribs and closed up the place. And from the rib God made a woman, and brought her to Adam.

When Adam woke up and saw her, he was so happy! “At last!” he said. “She is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” Here at last was someone just like him. Adam and the woman were husband and wife. Later Adam named her Eve.

So Adam and Eve lived in God’s beautiful garden. They had everything they needed. They had work to do, and each other to love. Best of all, God was with them. They were not afraid of Him, and they had nothing to hide. Everything was just the way God had made it to be.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 2

Dear God, thank you for giving us people to love, and good things to do. Thank you that you made us to be your friends. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did God use to make Adam, and how did Adam come alive?
study_questions.answer: God shaped Adam from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into him.

study_questions.question: What was the one rule in the garden?
study_questions.answer: Adam and Eve could eat from any tree except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

study_questions.question: God said it was not good for Adam to be alone. Who are the people God has given you to love?
study_questions.answer: Name family and friends together. God made us to need one another, and every one of them is a gift from Him.

fields.title: The Snake’s Trick
fields.body_html:
“But the LORD God called out to the man, ‘Where are you?’” — Genesis 3:9

In the garden there was a snake, and it was more cunning than any other animal. One day the snake came to Eve and asked a sly question.

“Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden’?”

That wasn’t what God had said at all. “We may eat fruit from the trees,” Eve answered. “But God said, ‘You must not eat from the tree in the middle of the garden, or even touch it, or you will die.’”

“You will not die,” said the snake. “God knows that when you eat it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

That was a lie. But Eve looked at the tree. The fruit looked good to eat, and lovely to look at, and she wanted to be wise. So she took some fruit and ate it. Adam was with her, and she gave some to him, and he ate it too.

At once everything changed. Adam and Eve felt ashamed. They sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves. And when they heard God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, they did something they had never done before. They hid from Him among the trees.

But God called out, “Where are you?”

God knew where they were. He was giving them the chance to come out and tell the truth. Adam came out, trembling. “I heard you in the garden,” he said, “and I was afraid, so I hid.”

“Did you eat from the tree I told you not to eat from?” God asked.

Adam blamed Eve. “The woman you gave me, she gave me the fruit.” And Eve blamed the snake. “The snake tricked me.” Nobody wanted to say, “It was my fault.”

Disobeying God is called sin, and sin spoils everything. Now there would be pain and hard work and sadness in the world. One day people would grow old and die. And Adam and Eve had to leave the beautiful garden.

But even on that sad day, God was kind. He made clothes out of animal skins for Adam and Eve and dressed them Himself. And He made a promise. He told the snake that one day a child would be born, a descendant of Eve, who would crush the snake’s head. The snake would hurt him, but He would win.

It was a promise that God would put things right. And the whole rest of the Bible is the story of God keeping that promise.

Looking ahead to Jesus: That promised child was Jesus. “This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 3

Dear God, I am sorry for the times I have disobeyed you and then hidden or blamed someone else. Thank you that you don’t stop loving me, and that you sent Jesus to put things right. Amen.

study_questions.question: What lie did the snake tell Eve?
study_questions.answer: The snake said she would not die if she ate the fruit, and that it would make her like God. It made God’s good rule sound like God was keeping something good from her.

study_questions.question: What did Adam and Eve do when they heard God coming?
study_questions.answer: They hid among the trees, and when God asked them what had happened, they blamed someone else.

study_questions.question: Why do you think we want to hide or blame someone else when we have done something wrong? What is the better thing to do?
study_questions.answer: We feel ashamed and afraid. The better thing is to come out and tell the truth, like God invited Adam to, because God is ready to forgive (1 John 1:9).

fields.title: Two Brothers
fields.body_html:
“If you do what is right, will you not be accepted?” — Genesis 4:7

After they left the garden, Adam and Eve had two sons. The older one was called Cain, and the younger one was called Abel.

When the boys grew up, Abel became a shepherd and looked after sheep. Cain became a farmer and grew crops in the fields.

One day both brothers brought a gift to God. Cain brought some of the food he had grown. Abel brought the very best from his flock, the first lambs that had been born. God was pleased with Abel and his gift. But He was not pleased with Cain and his gift.

The Bible doesn’t tell us everything about why. But it does tell us that Abel gave his gift with faith (Hebrews 11:4), trusting God and wanting to give Him the best. It seems Cain’s heart was not like that.

Cain was very angry. His face went dark and sulky.

God came to Cain and spoke to him kindly. “Why are you angry?” God asked. “If you do what is right, won’t you be accepted too? But be careful. Sin is waiting at your door like a hungry animal, ready to pounce. You must not let it win.”

God was giving Cain a warning, and a chance to change. But Cain didn’t listen.

One day Cain said to his brother, “Let’s go out to the field.” And when they were out in the field, far away from everyone, Cain attacked his brother Abel and killed him.

Then God asked Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?”

“I don’t know,” Cain lied. “Am I supposed to look after my brother?”

But God knew. “What have you done?” God said. Nothing can be hidden from God. Because of what he had done, Cain could no longer farm the land. He would have to wander from place to place.

Cain was frightened. “Someone will kill me,” he said.

And here is a surprising thing. Even though Cain had done something so terrible, God still took care of him. God put a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.

It is a very sad story. It shows how quickly sin grows. It started with jealousy and anger in Cain’s heart, and it ended with a brother dead. That is why God warned Cain to stop sin while it was still at the door. And it also shows that God is good and fair, and kind even to people who don’t deserve it.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible says that Jesus’ blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s death called out for justice. Jesus died to bring forgiveness.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 4:1–16

Dear God, when I feel jealous or angry, please help me to stop it before it grows. Thank you for your kindness, even when I don’t deserve it. Amen.

study_questions.question: What were Cain and Abel’s jobs, and what gifts did they bring to God?
study_questions.answer: Abel was a shepherd and brought the best of his first lambs. Cain was a farmer and brought some of his crops.

study_questions.question: What did God warn Cain about before anything bad happened?
study_questions.answer: God said sin was waiting at his door like an animal ready to pounce, and that Cain must not let it win.

study_questions.question: Has jealousy or anger ever made you want to do something unkind? What could you do when you feel that way?
study_questions.answer: Everyone feels jealous or angry sometimes. We can stop and pray, tell a grown-up, and ask God to help us before the feeling turns into something hurtful.

fields.title: Noah Builds a Boat
fields.body_html:
“So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.” — Genesis 6:22

As the years went by, there were more and more people in the world. But they were not like the people God had made them to be. They were cruel and violent, and they thought about doing wrong all the time. God was very sad. It hurt Him in His heart.

God decided that He would send a great flood to wash away all that wickedness. But there was one man who was different. His name was Noah. Noah loved God and walked with Him, and God was pleased with Noah.

God said to Noah, “Build yourself a boat, a huge one called an ark.” God told him exactly how to make it, out of wood and covered with tar to keep the water out. It was to be longer than a football pitch, with three floors inside, lots of rooms, a roof and a door in the side.

“I am going to send a flood,” God said. “But I will keep you safe. Go into the ark with your wife, and your three sons and their wives. And bring two of every kind of animal with you, a male and a female, to keep them alive.”

There wasn’t a cloud of trouble in the sky. People must have stared at Noah, building an enormous boat on dry land. But Noah trusted God. He did everything exactly as God told him.

When the ark was finished, the animals came. Two by two they came: cows and camels, foxes and frogs, eagles and elephants. Noah and his family stored up food for everyone. Then they all went inside, and God Himself shut the door.

Then it began to rain. And rain. And rain. Water burst up from under the ground too. It rained for forty days and forty nights. The water rose higher and higher until it covered the fields, then the houses, then even the tallest mountains. Everything that lived on the land and breathed the air died in the flood. But inside the ark, Noah and his family and all the animals floated safely on top of the water.

Then the rain stopped. “But God remembered Noah” (Genesis 8:1). He sent a wind, and slowly the water began to go down. One day the ark bumped to a stop on the mountains of Ararat.

Noah opened a window and sent out a dove to see if the land was dry. The dove came back, because there was nowhere to land. A week later he sent the dove out again. That evening she came back with a fresh olive leaf in her beak! Trees were growing again. A week after that he sent her out once more, and this time she didn’t come back at all.

At last God said, “Come out of the ark.” Out came Noah and his family, and out came all the animals, running and hopping and flying into a fresh, clean world.

Looking ahead to Jesus: Jesus said that one day He will come back, and it will be like the days of Noah (Matthew 24:37). Everyone who trusts Him will be safe with Him, just as Noah was safe in the ark.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 6–8

Dear God, thank you that you take care of people who trust you. Help me to listen to you and do what you say, like Noah did. Amen.

study_questions.answer: It can be hard. Talk about a real situation, like school or friends, and remember that God sees and is pleased when we trust Him, just as He was with Noah.

fields.title: The Rainbow Promise
fields.body_html:
“I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.” — Genesis 9:13

When Noah came out of the ark, the first thing he did was to build an altar and worship God. He was so thankful that God had kept his family safe through the flood.

God was pleased with Noah’s worship. And God made a promise.

“As long as the earth lasts,” God said, “there will always be planting and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night.”

Think about that. Every time the sun comes up in the morning, God is keeping His promise. Every time summer turns to autumn and autumn turns to winter, God is keeping His promise. Every time a farmer plants seeds and they grow into food, God is keeping His promise to Noah.

Then God blessed Noah and his sons. “Have lots of children,” He said, “and fill the earth.” The world had been empty after the flood, but now it would fill up with families again.

God told Noah that people are very precious to Him, because He made them in His own image. That is why nobody must ever take another person’s life.

Then God made a special promise, called a covenant, with Noah and his sons, and with every living creature: the birds and the cattle and all the wild animals that had come out of the ark.

“I promise you this,” God said. “Never again will a flood wipe out all life. Never again will a flood destroy the whole earth.”

And God gave them a sign to help them remember. He set His rainbow in the clouds.

“Whenever I bring clouds over the earth,” God said, “and the rainbow appears in the clouds, I will remember My promise between Me and you and every living creature. Never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all life.”

So the next time you see a rainbow, after a rain shower when the sun comes out, stop and look at it. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and all the colours in between, curving across the sky. That rainbow is a sign of God’s promise. God made a promise thousands of years ago, and He is still keeping it today.

God always keeps His promises. He kept His promise to Noah, and He will keep every promise He makes to you.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible says, “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Every promise God has ever made comes true because of Jesus.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 8:15–9:17

Dear God, thank you for the rainbow and for the seasons and for every sunrise. Thank you that you always keep your promises. Amen.

study_questions.question: What was the first thing Noah did when he came out of the ark?
study_questions.answer: He built an altar and worshipped God, thanking Him for keeping his family safe.

study_questions.question: What did God promise, and what sign did He give?
study_questions.answer: God promised that never again would a flood destroy all life on the earth. The rainbow in the clouds is the sign of that promise.

study_questions.question: What are some other promises God makes to us in the Bible?
study_questions.answer: For example, that He will never leave us (Hebrews 13:5), that He hears us when we pray, and that He forgives everyone who trusts in Jesus. Thank Him for one of them together.

fields.title: The Tower That Reached Too High
fields.body_html:
“That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world.” — Genesis 11:9

After the flood, Noah’s family grew and grew. Children were born, and then grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. And in those days everyone in the whole world spoke the same language. They all used the same words.

God had told people to spread out and fill the earth. But as they moved east, they came to a wide, flat plain in a land called Shinar, and they decided to settle down there.

They had discovered something new. Instead of using stones for building, they could make bricks out of mud and bake them hard in the fire. And they could stick the bricks together with tar.

“Come on,” they said to one another. “Let’s build ourselves a city, with a tower that reaches up to the sky! Then we’ll make a great name for ourselves. And we won’t be scattered all over the earth.”

Can you see what was wrong with their plan? They weren’t building to honour God. They wanted everyone to say how great they were. They wanted to make a name for themselves. And they wanted to stay together in one place, when God had told them to spread out over the world.

So they got to work. Brick on brick, higher and higher, the tower climbed towards the clouds. They must have been very proud of it.

But God came down to see the city and the tower they were building.

You see, the people thought their tower was enormous. But to God it was tiny. He had to come down to look at it! No tower, however tall, can ever reach up to God. God is far greater than anything people can build.

God said that if they could do this as one people speaking one language, nothing they planned would be beyond them. Their pride would only grow and grow. So God did something amazing. He mixed up their language.

All of a sudden, the builders couldn’t understand each other! One man would ask for more bricks, and his friend would hear nothing but strange sounds. Another would call for tar, and nobody knew what he meant. Imagine the muddle and the shouting!

They could not work together any more. So they had to stop building the city. People who could understand each other went off together, and they scattered all over the earth, just as God had wanted all along.

That city was called Babel, because it was where God confused the language of the whole world. And that is why there are so many different languages in the world today.

The people of Babel wanted to make a great name for themselves. But in the very next story, God chooses a man and promises, “I will make your name great.” Greatness is something God gives. We can’t grab it for ourselves.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 11:1–9

Dear God, you are greater than anything people can build. Please keep me from being proud and showing off, and help me to live for you and not for myself. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why did the people want to build the tower?
study_questions.answer: To make a great name for themselves and to stay together in one place, even though God had told them to spread out over the earth.

study_questions.question: What did God do to stop the building?
study_questions.answer: He mixed up their language, so they couldn’t understand each other, and they scattered all over the earth.

study_questions.question: When do you feel like showing off? How could you give the praise to God instead?
study_questions.answer: Perhaps when you are good at something or win a game. We can thank God for the gifts He has given us, and use them to help others.

fields.title: Abram Sets Out
fields.body_html:
“Then the LORD said to Abram, ‘Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you.’” — Genesis 12:1

Many years after the tower of Babel, there lived a man named Abram. He lived in a town called Haran with his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot.

One day God spoke to Abram. “Leave your country and your relatives and your father’s family,” God said, “and go to the land I will show you.”

God didn’t tell Abram where the land was. He didn’t give him a map. He just said, “Go, and I will show you.”

And then God made Abram some wonderful promises. “I will make you into a great nation,” God said. “I will bless you, and I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”

That was an amazing promise. Abram and Sarai didn’t have any children at all. How could they become a great nation? And how could the whole world be blessed through one man and his wife?

But Abram trusted God. He didn’t argue, and he didn’t wait to find out more. The Bible says, “So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him” (Genesis 12:4). He was seventy-five years old!

So Abram packed up everything he owned. There were tents and pots, sheep and goats, cattle and donkeys, and all the people who worked for him. Sarai came, and so did Lot. And off they went, a long line of people and animals, walking south across the dusty land.

Day after day they travelled, until at last they came to a land called Canaan. There, at a place called Shechem, by a great tree, God appeared to Abram again.

“I will give this land to your children,” God said.

Abram still didn’t have any children. But he believed God. So right there he built an altar out of stones and worshipped God, who had brought him all that way.

Then Abram moved on through the land, living in tents. Wherever he went, he built an altar and prayed to God and worshipped Him. Abram didn’t have a house or a city of his own. But he had something better. He had God’s promises, and he had God Himself with him.

The Bible says that Abram “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). That is what it means to trust God. We don’t always know what is going to happen next, but we know God, and that is enough.

Looking ahead to Jesus: God promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abram. The Bible tells us that this promise came true in Jesus, Abram’s great-great-great-grandson many times over, who came to bless people from every nation in the world (Galatians 3:8, 16).

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 12:1–9

Dear God, thank you that I can trust you even when I don’t know what will happen next. Help me to follow you wherever you lead me. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did God tell Abram to do?
study_questions.answer: To leave his country and his family and go to a land God would show him, without telling him where it was.

study_questions.question: What did God promise Abram?
study_questions.answer: To make him into a great nation, to bless him and make his name great, and to bless all the families of the earth through him.

study_questions.question: Abram had to trust God without knowing what would happen. Is there something new or scary coming up for you where you could trust God?
study_questions.answer: Maybe a new school, a move, or a hard day. Pray about it together, and remember that God goes with you just as He went with Abram.

fields.title: Count the Stars
fields.body_html:
“Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” — Genesis 15:6

Abram had been living in the land of Canaan for a long time. God had blessed him. He had lots of sheep and cattle and silver and gold. But there was one thing Abram didn’t have. He and Sarai still had no children.

One night, God spoke to Abram in a vision. “Do not be afraid, Abram,” God said. “I am your shield, and your very great reward.”

But Abram was sad. “Lord God,” he said, “what can you give me? I still don’t have any children. When I die, everything I have will go to my servant Eliezer.”

“No,” God said. “That man will not be the one. You will have a son of your very own, and he will be the one.”

Then God took Abram outside, into the dark night.

Have you ever been somewhere really dark, far away from any towns or street lights, and looked up at the sky? There are stars everywhere. Thousands and thousands of them, big ones and tiny ones, so many that the sky looks dusty with them.

That is what Abram saw that night.

“Look up at the sky,” God said, “and count the stars, if you can.”

So Abram looked. One, two, three, four... But he could never count them all. Nobody could.

“That is how many children and grandchildren and great-grandchildren you will have,” God said.

Abram was an old man. Sarai was an old woman. They had waited and waited for a baby, and no baby had come. It seemed impossible.

But Abram looked up at all those stars, and he believed God.

That is a very short sentence in the Bible, but it is one of the most important ones. “Abram believed the LORD.” He trusted that God would do what He had promised, even when he couldn’t see how. And God was pleased with Abram’s faith. Because Abram trusted Him, God counted him as right with Him, as His friend.

That is still the way people become God’s friends today. Not by being good enough, but by trusting God, just as Abram did.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible says, “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Galatians 3:29). Everyone who trusts in Jesus becomes part of Abram’s family. So if you trust Jesus, you are one of those stars!

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 15:1–6

Dear God, thank you that you always keep your promises, even when they seem impossible. Help me to trust you like Abram did. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why was Abram sad when God spoke to him?
study_questions.answer: Because he and Sarai still didn’t have any children, and he thought everything he owned would go to his servant.

study_questions.question: What did God show Abram, and what did it mean?
study_questions.answer: God showed him the stars, which were too many to count. It meant Abram would have more children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren than he could ever count.

study_questions.question: What does it mean to believe God, like Abram did?
study_questions.answer: It means trusting that God will do what He has said, even when we can’t see how. That is how we become God’s friends: by trusting Him, especially by trusting Jesus.

fields.title: Sarah Laughs
fields.body_html:
“Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” — Genesis 18:14

God gave Abram and Sarai new names. Abram became Abraham, which means “father of many”. And Sarai became Sarah, which means “princess”. But they still had no baby. Abraham was nearly one hundred years old now, and Sarah was almost ninety.

One very hot day, Abraham was sitting at the entrance of his tent, under some big oak trees. He looked up, and there were three men standing nearby.

Abraham jumped up and ran to meet them, and bowed down low. “Please stay,” he said. “Let me bring you some water to wash your feet, and you can rest under the tree. I’ll get you something to eat.”

Then Abraham hurried into the tent. “Quick, Sarah!” he said. “Bake some bread!” He ran to his herd and chose a good, tender calf for a servant to cook. And soon he set out a feast for his visitors, with milk and curds and the meat, and stood near them under the tree while they ate.

These were not ordinary visitors. One of them was God Himself, come to visit Abraham.

“Where is your wife Sarah?” they asked.

“There, in the tent,” said Abraham.

“I will come back to you this time next year,” said the Lord, “and your wife Sarah will have a son.”

Now Sarah was inside the tent, just behind the doorway, listening. And when she heard that, she laughed to herself. “Me? Have a baby?” she thought. “I’m far too old for that. And so is my husband!”

Then the Lord said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh? Why did she say, ‘Can I really have a baby when I’m old?’ Is anything too difficult for the Lord? I will come back next year, and Sarah will have a son.”

Sarah was frightened. “I didn’t laugh,” she said.

“Yes, you did laugh,” said the Lord.

“God has made me laugh,” she said, “and everyone who hears about this will laugh with me. Who would ever have said to Abraham that Sarah would feed a baby? But I have had a son in his old age!”

God had made a promise that seemed impossible. And He kept it. Nothing is too difficult for the Lord.

fields.title: The God Who Sees
fields.body_html:
“You are the God who sees me.” — Genesis 16:13

Before Isaac was born, while Sarah was still waiting for a baby, she had an idea. It was not a good idea, and it was not God’s way.

Sarah had a servant girl from Egypt called Hagar. “God hasn’t given me any children,” Sarah said to Abraham. “So take Hagar as your wife too, and her children can be mine.” Abraham agreed. Soon Hagar was expecting a baby.

But then Hagar began to look down on Sarah. And Sarah became angry and treated Hagar so harshly that Hagar ran away, out into the desert.

Hagar was alone. She was far from home. Nobody was looking for her, and she was going to have a baby. She stopped beside a spring of water in the wilderness.

But someone had come looking for her. The angel of the Lord found Hagar by the spring.

“Hagar,” he said, “where have you come from, and where are you going?”

“I’m running away from Sarah,” she said.

The angel told her to go back. And he gave her a promise. “You are going to have a son,” he said. “You must call him Ishmael, which means ‘God hears’, because the Lord has heard about your trouble.”

Hagar was amazed. Nobody else had noticed her. But God had seen her. So she gave God a name. She said, “You are the God who sees me.”

So Hagar went back, and she had a baby boy, and she called him Ishmael.

Years later, after Isaac was born, there was trouble again in the family. Sarah wanted Hagar and Ishmael to leave. Abraham was very upset, because Ishmael was his son too. But God told Abraham, “Don’t be upset. I will take care of the boy and make his family into a nation too.”

So early in the morning, Abraham gave Hagar some bread and a skin bag full of water, and sent her and Ishmael away.

They wandered in the desert. The sun beat down. And then the water ran out. Hagar laid her boy down in the shade of a bush, and went and sat a little way off. “I can’t watch my son die,” she said. And she began to cry.

But God heard the boy crying. The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven. “What is wrong, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy.” Then God opened Hagar’s eyes, and she saw a well of water! She filled the bag and gave her son a drink.

God was with Ishmael as he grew up in the desert. He became an expert with a bow and arrow, and in time he had a big family of his own.

Hagar was a servant. She was far from home, and people had treated her badly. But God saw her and heard her son, both times. Nobody is too small for God to notice.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 16; 21:8–21

Dear God, thank you that you see me and hear me, even when I feel alone. Please help people who are lonely or far from home today. Amen.

study_questions.question: Where did the angel of the Lord find Hagar the first time?
study_questions.answer: By a spring of water in the desert, after she had run away from Sarah.

study_questions.question: What name did Hagar give to God, and what does Ishmael’s name mean?
study_questions.answer: She called Him “the God who sees me”. Ishmael means “God hears”.

study_questions.question: Have you ever felt like nobody noticed you? How does it help to know that God sees you?
study_questions.answer: Everyone feels left out sometimes. God sees us all the time and cares about us, even when no one else seems to. We can also notice other people who feel left out, and be kind to them.

fields.title: God Will Provide
fields.body_html:
“Abraham answered, ‘God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.’” — Genesis 22:8

Isaac grew from a baby into a boy. Abraham and Sarah loved him so much. He was the son God had promised, the one through whom all those starry promises would come true.

Then one day God tested Abraham. “Abraham!” God called.

“Here I am,” Abraham answered.

“Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love,” God said, “and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there to me as a sacrifice on a mountain I will show you.”

In those days, people gave gifts to God called sacrifices. They would kill an animal, like a lamb, and burn it on an altar. But now God was asking for Isaac.

This is one of the hardest stories in the Bible. Abraham must have been heartbroken. But he didn’t argue. Early the next morning, he cut wood for the fire, loaded up his donkey, and set out with Isaac and two servants.

On the third day Abraham saw the mountain in the distance. He told the servants, “Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go up there and worship, and then we will come back to you.” Did you notice? Abraham said “we will come back”.

Abraham put the wood on Isaac’s back, and he carried the fire and the knife. And the two of them walked on together.

“Father?” said Isaac.

“Here I am, my son.”

“We’ve got the fire and the wood,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb?”

“God Himself will provide the lamb, my son,” said Abraham. And the two of them walked on together.

When they reached the top of the mountain, Abraham built an altar and laid the wood on it. He tied up Isaac and laid him on the altar. Then he reached out for the knife.

But at that very moment, the angel of the Lord called out from heaven. “Abraham! Abraham!”

“Here I am.”

“Do not lay a hand on the boy!” said the angel. “Now I know that you fear God, because you have not held back your son, your only son, from Me.”

Abraham looked up, and there in a bush was a ram, a big male sheep, caught by its horns. Abraham untied Isaac. Then he took the ram and offered it to God instead of his son.

Abraham called that place “The Lord Will Provide”.

God never wanted Isaac to die. He stopped Abraham, just as Abraham had trusted He would. The Bible tells us that Abraham believed God could even bring Isaac back from the dead if He had to (Hebrews 11:19). Abraham trusted that God would keep His promise, whatever happened.

And God did provide. He gave a ram to take Isaac’s place.

Looking ahead to Jesus: Hundreds of years later, God did provide the Lamb. When John the Baptist saw Jesus, he said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). God stopped Abraham from giving up his son. But God “did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Jesus took our place, like the ram took Isaac’s.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 22:1–19

Dear God, thank you that you provide everything we need. Thank you most of all for giving Jesus, your only Son, to take my place. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Isaac ask his father on the way up the mountain, and what did Abraham answer?
study_questions.answer: Isaac asked, “Where is the lamb?” Abraham answered, “God Himself will provide the lamb, my son.”

study_questions.question: How did God stop Abraham, and what did He provide?
study_questions.answer: The angel of the Lord called out from heaven and told him not to hurt the boy. Then God provided a ram caught in a bush to be offered instead of Isaac.

study_questions.question: How is Jesus like the ram on the mountain?
study_questions.answer: The ram died in Isaac’s place. Jesus, the Lamb of God, died in our place, to take away our sin. This story can raise big questions, so let your child ask whatever they want to, and remind them that God never wanted Isaac to die.

fields.title: A Bride at the Well
fields.body_html:
“‘O LORD, God of my master Abraham,’ he prayed, ‘please grant me success today.’” — Genesis 24:12

Isaac grew up to be a man, and Abraham grew very old. Sarah had died, and Isaac missed his mother very much. Abraham wanted Isaac to have a wife. But not a wife from the people of Canaan, who worshipped false gods. He wanted her to come from his own family, far away in the land where he used to live.

So Abraham called his oldest and most trusted servant. “Go to my homeland and my relatives,” Abraham said, “and find a wife for my son Isaac. God will send His angel ahead of you.”

The servant took ten of Abraham’s camels, loaded with all kinds of fine gifts, and set off on the long journey. When at last he arrived at the town where Abraham’s relatives lived, it was evening. He made the camels kneel down beside the well outside the town. It was the time when the girls came out to fetch water.

The servant didn’t know what to do next. So he prayed.

“O Lord, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “please give me success today. I’m standing here by the well. Let it be like this. I will say to one of the girls, ‘Please give me a drink from your jar.’ If she says, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels too,’ let her be the one you have chosen for Isaac.”

That was a big thing to ask. Camels drink a huge amount of water, especially after a long journey, and there were ten of them!

Before he had even finished praying, a beautiful young woman came out with a water jar on her shoulder. Her name was Rebekah. She went down to the well and filled her jar.

The servant ran to meet her. “Please give me a little water from your jar,” he said.

“Drink, sir,” she said, and quickly lowered her jar so he could drink. Then she said, “I’ll draw water for your camels too, until they’ve had enough.” And she ran back and forth to the well, again and again, until all ten camels had finished drinking.

The servant watched her in amazement. When the camels had finished, he gave her a gold ring and two gold bracelets. “Whose daughter are you?” he asked.

And it turned out that Rebekah was the granddaughter of Abraham’s own brother!

The servant bowed down and worshipped God right there. “Blessed be the Lord, the God of my master Abraham,” he said. “The Lord has led me straight to the house of my master’s relatives!”

Rebekah’s family welcomed him, and he told them the whole story. They could see that God had arranged everything. So they called Rebekah and asked her, “Will you go with this man?”

“I will go,” she said.

So Rebekah travelled all the way back to Canaan. One evening, Isaac was out walking in the field when he looked up and saw camels coming. Rebekah became Isaac’s wife, and he loved her. And she comforted him after his mother’s death.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 24

Dear God, thank you that I can pray to you about anything, big or small. Please guide me, the way you guided Abraham’s servant. And help me to be kind and helpful like Rebekah. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Abraham’s servant pray for at the well?
study_questions.answer: He asked God for success, and that the girl God had chosen for Isaac would offer to water his camels as well as give him a drink.

study_questions.question: How did Rebekah show that she was kind and hard-working?
study_questions.answer: She gave the servant a drink and then ran back and forth to the well again and again until all ten thirsty camels had had enough.

study_questions.question: The servant prayed before he did anything else. What is something you could ask God to guide you in?
study_questions.answer: Choose something real together, like a friendship, a decision or a worry, and pray about it. Then watch for how God answers.

fields.title: Twin Brothers
fields.body_html:
“When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home.” — Genesis 25:27

Isaac and Rebekah waited a long time for children. Isaac prayed for his wife, and God answered his prayer. Rebekah was going to have twins!

Even before they were born, the twins struggled and pushed inside her. God told Rebekah, “Two nations are inside you. One will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”

The first baby to be born was red all over and covered in hair, so they called him Esau. Then his twin brother came out, holding on to Esau’s heel! They called him Jacob, which sounds like the word for “heel” and means “he grabs”.

The boys grew up very different. Esau loved to be outdoors, hunting wild animals. Jacob was quiet and liked to stay at home among the tents. Isaac loved Esau best, because he loved eating the meat Esau brought home. But Rebekah loved Jacob best.

In those days the oldest son had a special place in the family, called the birthright. He would get the biggest share of everything when his father died, and he would lead the family.

One day Jacob was cooking a pot of red lentil stew. Esau came in from the fields, very hungry. “Quick, give me some of that red stew!” he said. “I’m starving!”

“First sell me your birthright,” said Jacob.

“Look, I’m about to die of hunger,” said Esau. “What good is a birthright to me?” So Esau promised his birthright to Jacob in exchange for a bowl of stew and some bread. He ate, and drank, and went on his way. Esau didn’t care about the special gift God had given him.

Years later, when Isaac was very old and couldn’t see any more, he called Esau. “Go and hunt for some meat and make me my favourite meal,” he said. “Then I will give you my blessing before I die.”

Rebekah overheard. She wanted the blessing for Jacob instead, so she made a plan. She cooked the meal herself. She dressed Jacob in Esau’s clothes, and put goatskins on his hands and neck so that he would feel hairy like his brother. Then Jacob took the food to his father.

“I am Esau, your firstborn,” Jacob lied.

Isaac felt his hands. “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands,” he said. And he gave Jacob the blessing.

Soon afterwards Esau came in with his meal. When he found out what had happened, he let out a loud and bitter cry. “Bless me too, my father!” But the blessing had already been given.

Esau was so angry that he planned to kill his brother. So Jacob had to run away from home, all the way to his uncle Laban in Haran, far away.

The family was full of favourites and tricks and lies, and it ended in tears. But even in the middle of all that mess, God’s plan didn’t fail. God had said that the older would serve the younger. And God was not finished with Jacob yet.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 25:19–34; 27

Dear God, help me to be honest even when I want something very much. Thank you that your plans don’t fail, even when people get things wrong. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Esau swap his birthright for?
study_questions.answer: A bowl of red lentil stew and some bread, because he was hungry and didn’t care about his birthright.

study_questions.question: How did Jacob trick his father?
study_questions.answer: He wore Esau’s clothes and put goatskins on his hands and neck so he felt hairy, brought the meal his mother had cooked, and said he was Esau.

study_questions.question: Jacob got what he wanted by lying, but it made a terrible mess. Why does lying cause so much trouble?
study_questions.answer: Lies break trust and hurt people, even when we get what we want. Jacob had to leave his home and family. We can ask God to help us tell the truth, even when it is hard.

fields.title: A Stairway to Heaven
fields.body_html:
“When Jacob woke up, he said, ‘Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.’” — Genesis 28:16

Jacob was running away. His brother Esau was furious with him, so he had left home and was walking all the way to his uncle Laban’s house, hundreds of miles away.

He was all alone. He had tricked his father and his brother, and now he had nothing but the clothes he was wearing and a walking stick.

As the sun went down, Jacob stopped for the night. There was no house and no bed, so he took a stone, put it under his head for a pillow, and lay down to sleep in the open.

And while he slept, Jacob had a dream.

He saw a stairway, or a ladder, standing on the earth, with its top reaching all the way up to heaven. And God’s angels were going up and down on it!

And there, above it, stood the Lord. “I am the Lord,” He said, “the God of your grandfather Abraham and the God of your father Isaac. I will give you and your children the land you are lying on. Your family will be as many as the specks of dust on the ground. They will spread out in every direction. And all the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your children.”

It was the same promise God had made to Abraham. And then God said something just for Jacob.

“Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.”

Jacob didn’t deserve that. He had lied and cheated. He was running away. But God came to him anyway, and made him a promise full of grace.

When Jacob woke up, he said, “Surely the Lord is in this place, and I didn’t know it!” He was amazed and a little afraid. “This is none other than the house of God,” he said. “This is the gate of heaven!”

Early in the morning, Jacob took the stone he had used as a pillow and set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it, to mark the special place where God had met him. He named the place Bethel, which means “house of God”.

Then Jacob made a promise of his own. “If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey,” he said, “and give me food to eat and clothes to wear, and bring me safely home, then the Lord will be my God.”

Jacob still had a lot to learn. But God had found him, out there in the middle of nowhere. And God would keep His promise to be with him wherever he went.

Looking ahead to Jesus: Jesus told His friends, “You will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Jesus is the true stairway between heaven and earth. He is the way we can come to God.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 28:10–22

Dear God, thank you that you are with me wherever I go, even when I don’t realise it. Thank you that Jesus makes the way for me to come to you. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Jacob see in his dream?
study_questions.answer: A stairway reaching from the earth up to heaven, with God’s angels going up and down on it, and the Lord standing above it.

study_questions.question: What did God promise Jacob?
study_questions.answer: That He would be with him, watch over him wherever he went, bring him home again, and never leave him until He had done everything He had promised.

study_questions.question: Jacob didn’t deserve God’s kindness, but God came to him anyway. What does that tell us about God?
study_questions.answer: That God is full of grace. He loves and helps people who don’t deserve it, and that includes all of us. We can thank Him for His kindness to us.

fields.title: Jacob Wrestles
fields.body_html:
“But Jacob replied, ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’” — Genesis 32:26

Jacob lived with his uncle Laban for twenty years. He married two sisters, Leah and Rachel, and had a big family of eleven sons and a daughter. He had huge flocks of sheep and goats. But at last God told him, “Go back home to the land of your fathers, and I will be with you.”

So Jacob set off for home with his whole family and all his animals. But there was one big problem. Esau.

Jacob sent messengers ahead to tell Esau he was coming. They came back with frightening news. “Your brother Esau is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him!”

Jacob was terrified. Was Esau still angry? Was he coming to attack?

Jacob did what he should have done long ago. He prayed. “O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac,” he said, “I am not worthy of all the kindness and faithfulness you have shown me. When I crossed this river years ago, I had only a walking stick. Now I have two whole camps of people and animals. Please save me from my brother Esau. I am afraid. But you promised to be good to me.”

Then Jacob sent hundreds of goats and sheep, camels and cows and donkeys ahead as presents for Esau. That night he sent his family safely across the stream, and he was left alone.

And in the dark, a man came and wrestled with him. They wrestled all night long, rolling in the dust, until the sky began to grow light. The man could not win, so he touched Jacob’s hip, and it was wrenched out of joint. It must have hurt badly. But Jacob still held on.

“Let me go,” said the man, “for it is daybreak.”

But Jacob said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

“What is your name?” the man asked.

“Jacob,” he answered. Jacob, the one who grabs. The trickster.

“Your name will no longer be Jacob,” said the man, “but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with people, and you have won.” And he blessed Jacob there.

Jacob realised who he had been wrestling with. “I have seen God face to face,” he said, “and yet my life was spared!” As the sun rose, Jacob limped on his way.

Then he looked up and saw Esau coming, with his four hundred men. Jacob went ahead of his family, bowing down to the ground seven times as he came near his brother.

But Esau ran to meet him. He threw his arms around Jacob’s neck and kissed him. And they both cried.

After all those years, God had changed Jacob, and God had softened Esau’s heart. The brothers were friends again.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 32–33

Dear God, thank you that I can hold on to you when I am afraid. Please help me to make up with people I have hurt, and help them to forgive me. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why was Jacob so afraid of going home?
study_questions.answer: Because he had tricked his brother Esau twenty years before, and now Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men.

study_questions.question: What new name did Jacob get, and what happened when he met Esau?
study_questions.answer: His new name was Israel, because he had struggled with God and won. When he met Esau, Esau ran to him and hugged him, and they both cried.

study_questions.question: Is there anyone you need to say sorry to, or make up with?
study_questions.answer: Talk about it gently. Saying sorry can be scary, like it was for Jacob. We can pray first, like Jacob did, and ask God to help.

fields.title: Joseph’s Colourful Robe
fields.body_html:
“Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons ... so he made him a robe of many colors.” — Genesis 37:3

Jacob, who was now called Israel, had twelve sons. But his favourite was Joseph. Joseph was the son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved most, and he was born when Jacob was old. Jacob made Joseph a special robe, a beautiful coat of many colours.

When Joseph was seventeen, he looked after the sheep with his older brothers. But his brothers hated him. They could see that their father loved Joseph more than any of them, and they couldn’t even say a kind word to him.

Then Joseph had a dream, and he told his brothers about it. “Listen to this dream I had,” he said. “We were tying up bundles of wheat in the field. Suddenly my bundle stood up straight, and all your bundles gathered round it and bowed down to mine!”

“So you think you’re going to be king over us, do you?” his brothers said. And they hated him even more.

Then Joseph had another dream. “This time,” he said, “the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” Even his father told him off for that one.

One day the brothers were far away, looking after the sheep. Jacob sent Joseph to find out how they were doing. Joseph walked a long way, and at last he saw them in the distance.

His brothers saw him coming too, in his colourful robe. “Here comes that dreamer!” they said to one another. “Come on, let’s kill him and throw him into a pit. We’ll say a wild animal ate him. Then we’ll see what becomes of his dreams!”

But Reuben, the oldest brother, said, “Don’t kill him. Just throw him into this empty pit.” Reuben secretly planned to come back and rescue Joseph later.

So when Joseph arrived, they grabbed him and pulled off his beautiful robe. They threw him into a deep, dry pit. And then they sat down to eat their lunch.

While they were eating, they saw a long line of camels coming. They were traders, carrying spices down to Egypt.

Judah, another brother, had an idea. “What will we get if we kill our brother?” he said. “Let’s sell him to these traders instead.” So they pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty pieces of silver. And the traders took Joseph away to Egypt.

Then the brothers killed a goat and dipped Joseph’s robe in its blood. They took it home to their father. “We found this,” they said. “Is it Joseph’s robe?”

Jacob knew it at once. “A wild animal has eaten him!” he cried. He tore his clothes and wept, and nobody could comfort him.

It looked as if everything had gone wrong. Joseph was gone, a slave in a faraway land. But God had not forgotten Joseph. And God had not forgotten Joseph’s dreams.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 37

Dear God, please help me not to be jealous when someone else gets something I want. And when things go wrong, help me to remember that you haven’t forgotten me. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why did Joseph’s brothers hate him?
study_questions.answer: Because their father loved Joseph more than them and gave him a special robe, and because of Joseph’s dreams about them bowing down to him.

study_questions.question: What did the brothers do to Joseph, and what did they tell their father?
study_questions.answer: They threw him into a pit and then sold him to traders going to Egypt. They dipped his robe in goat’s blood so their father would think a wild animal had killed him.

study_questions.question: Jealousy made the brothers do something terrible. What could have stopped it?
study_questions.answer: If they had told the truth about their feelings, or listened to Reuben, or asked God for help, things could have been different. Jealousy grows when we feed it, just like Cain’s did, so it’s best to deal with it early.

fields.title: Joseph in Prison
fields.body_html:
“The LORD was with him and extended kindness to him.” — Genesis 39:21

In Egypt, Joseph was sold to a man called Potiphar, an important officer of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. Joseph was a slave now, far from home and his father. But the Bible says something wonderful: “The LORD was with Joseph” (Genesis 39:2).

Joseph worked hard, and God made everything he did go well. Potiphar saw it, and he put Joseph in charge of his whole house. God blessed Potiphar’s house because of Joseph.

But Potiphar’s wife began to cause trouble. Joseph was handsome, and day after day she tried to get Joseph to love her, the way only her husband should. Joseph always said no. “My master trusts me with everything,” he said. “How could I do such a wicked thing and sin against God?”

One day, when nobody else was in the house, she grabbed Joseph by his cloak. Joseph ran away, leaving his cloak in her hand. So she told lies about him. She showed the cloak to everyone and said Joseph had attacked her.

Potiphar was furious. And he threw Joseph into prison.

That doesn’t seem fair, does it? Joseph had done the right thing, and he was punished for it. But even in prison, the Lord was with Joseph and was kind to him. Soon the prison warden put Joseph in charge of all the other prisoners.

One day two new prisoners arrived. One was Pharaoh’s cupbearer, who served the king his drinks. The other was Pharaoh’s baker. One morning Joseph found them both looking very upset.

“Why are you so sad today?” asked Joseph.

“We both had dreams,” they said, “and there’s no one to tell us what they mean.”

“Don’t interpretations belong to God?” said Joseph. “Tell me your dreams.”

The cupbearer went first. “I saw a vine with three branches,” he said. “It budded and blossomed, and grapes grew on it. I squeezed the grapes into Pharaoh’s cup and gave it to him.”

God showed Joseph what it meant. “The three branches are three days,” Joseph said. “In three days, Pharaoh will give you your job back. And when that happens, please remember me. Tell Pharaoh about me and get me out of this prison, because I’ve done nothing wrong.”

The baker’s dream had a sadder meaning. In three days, said Joseph, the baker would be put to death.

Three days later it was Pharaoh’s birthday. Everything happened just as Joseph had said. The cupbearer got his job back, and the baker was put to death.

But the cupbearer forgot all about Joseph.

Joseph stayed in prison for two more whole years. He must have wondered whether anyone would ever remember him. But God remembered him. And God was getting ready to do something amazing.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 39–40

Dear God, help me to do what is right even when nobody else is. And when I have to wait, help me to trust that you are with me and haven’t forgotten me. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why was Joseph thrown into prison?
study_questions.answer: Because Potiphar’s wife told lies about him after Joseph refused to do wrong with her and ran away.

study_questions.question: What did Joseph say when the cupbearer and the baker told him they had no one to explain their dreams?
study_questions.answer: He said, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams.” He knew that only God could give the meaning.

study_questions.question: Joseph did the right thing and still got into trouble. How did God take care of him?
study_questions.answer: God was with Joseph in prison, was kind to him, and made the warden put him in charge. Doing right doesn’t always make life easy, but God never leaves us.

fields.title: Pharaoh’s Dreams
fields.body_html:
“‘I myself cannot do it,’ Joseph replied, ‘but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer.’” — Genesis 41:16

Two whole years went by. Then one night Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, had two strange dreams.

In the first dream, he was standing by the River Nile. Seven fat, healthy cows came up out of the river and ate the grass. Then seven more cows came up after them, thin and bony and ugly. And the seven thin cows ate up the seven fat cows!

Pharaoh woke up. Then he fell asleep again, and had another dream. Seven heads of grain, plump and good, were growing on one stalk. Then seven more heads of grain sprouted, thin and dried up by the hot wind. And the thin heads of grain swallowed up the good ones!

In the morning Pharaoh was worried. He called all the magicians and wise men of Egypt and told them his dreams. But nobody could tell him what they meant.

Then the cupbearer suddenly remembered. “Today I remember my mistakes,” he said to Pharaoh. And he told Pharaoh about the young Hebrew man in prison who had explained his dream, and how everything had happened just as he said.

Pharaoh sent for Joseph at once. They hurried him out of the prison. He shaved and changed his clothes, and then he stood before the king of Egypt.

“I had a dream, and no one can tell me what it means,” said Pharaoh. “I hear that you can explain dreams.”

“I myself cannot do it,” said Joseph, “but God will give Pharaoh a good answer.”

Joseph didn’t want any praise for himself. He wanted Pharaoh to know that God was the One who knew the answer.

Pharaoh told Joseph his dreams. And God showed Joseph what they meant.

“The two dreams mean the same thing,” said Joseph. “God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do. The seven fat cows and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. There will be seven years of plenty, with lots of food all over Egypt. Then the seven thin cows and the seven dried-up heads of grain are seven more years. There will be seven years of famine, when nothing grows, and people will be terribly hungry.”

Then Joseph gave Pharaoh some advice. “Find a wise man and put him in charge of Egypt. During the good years, store up some of the food. Then there will be enough to eat when the famine comes.”

Pharaoh was amazed. “Can we find anyone like this man, who has the Spirit of God in him?” he said. Then he turned to Joseph. “Since God has shown you all this, there is no one as wise as you. You shall be in charge of my palace and all my people. Only I, as king, will be greater than you.”

Pharaoh put his own ring on Joseph’s finger. He dressed him in fine clothes and put a gold chain around his neck, and gave him a chariot to ride in. Joseph was thirty years old. That morning he had been a prisoner. By evening he was the most important man in Egypt after the king!

For seven years the harvests were huge, and Joseph stored up so much grain that it was like the sand on the seashore. There was too much to count. Then the famine came, just as God had said. But Egypt had plenty of food, because God had given Joseph wisdom.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 41

Dear God, thank you that you know everything that is going to happen. When I do something well, help me to give the praise to you, like Joseph did. Amen.

study_questions.question: What were Pharaoh’s two dreams about?
study_questions.answer: Seven fat cows eaten by seven thin cows, and seven good heads of grain swallowed by seven thin ones.

study_questions.question: What did the dreams mean, and what was Joseph’s plan?
study_questions.answer: Seven years of plenty, then seven years of famine. Joseph said Egypt should store up food during the good years so there would be enough in the famine.

study_questions.question: Joseph said, “I cannot do it, but God will.” Why was that a good thing to say?
study_questions.answer: Because it was true, and it gave the glory to God instead of to himself. When we are good at something, we can remember that our gifts come from God.

For seven years the harvests were huge, and Joseph stored up so much grain that it was like the sand on the seashore. There was too much to count. Then the famine came, just as God had said. But Egypt had plenty of food, because God had given Joseph wisdom. Read it in your Bible: Genesis 41 Dear God, thank you that you know everything that is going to happen. When I do something well, help me to give the praise to you, like Joseph did. Amen.

fields.title: The Brothers Come to Egypt
fields.body_html:
“Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy.” — Genesis 44:33

The famine spread far beyond Egypt. Back in Canaan, Jacob and his family were running out of food. Then Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt.

“Go down there and buy some grain for us,” Jacob told his sons, “so that we don’t die.” So ten of Joseph’s brothers set off for Egypt. But Jacob kept the youngest, Benjamin, at home. Benjamin was Joseph’s only full brother, and now he was Jacob’s favourite. Jacob couldn’t bear to lose him too.

In Egypt, the brothers came to the governor who was in charge of selling grain, and they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.

The governor was Joseph! He knew his brothers at once. But they didn’t recognise him at all. Joseph was grown up now, and he was dressed like an Egyptian and spoke Egyptian. And Joseph remembered his dreams about his brothers bowing down to him.

Joseph decided to test them. Were they still the same cruel men who had sold him? He spoke to them harshly. “You are spies!” he said.

“No, my lord!” they said. “We are honest men. We were twelve brothers. The youngest is at home with our father, and one is no more.”

“Then prove it,” said Joseph. “One of you must stay here in prison. The rest of you go home with grain, and bring your youngest brother back to me.”

The brothers said to one another, “This is happening because of what we did to Joseph. We saw how upset he was when he begged us to let him go, but we wouldn’t listen.”

They didn’t know that Joseph could understand every word. Joseph turned away from them and cried.

Joseph kept Simeon in prison and sent the others home with sacks full of grain. When the grain ran out, Jacob had no choice. He had to let Benjamin go. Judah promised his father, “I will take care of him myself. If I don’t bring him back, you can blame me for ever.”

When the brothers came back to Egypt with Benjamin, Joseph gave them a feast. Then he tested them one last time. He had his own silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack of grain. When the brothers had set off for home, Joseph’s servant chased after them and searched the sacks. And there was the cup, in Benjamin’s sack!

The brothers were horrified. They went back to Joseph and threw themselves on the ground.

“The one who had the cup will be my slave,” said Joseph. “The rest of you can go home.”

This was the real test. Years before, they had let their father’s favourite son be taken away as a slave. Would they do it again?

Judah stepped forward. “Please, my lord,” he said. “If we go home without the boy, our father will die of sadness. Please let me stay here as your slave instead of him. Let the boy go home with his brothers.”

Judah, who had once sold Joseph as a slave, was now ready to become a slave himself to save his brother. The brothers had changed.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 42–44

Dear God, thank you that you can change people’s hearts. Please change my heart too, and make me ready to help and protect others. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why didn’t Joseph’s brothers recognise him?
study_questions.answer: He was grown up, dressed like an Egyptian, spoke Egyptian, and was the governor of Egypt. They thought he was a slave, or dead.

study_questions.question: What did Judah offer to do when the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack?
study_questions.answer: He offered to stay in Egypt as a slave in Benjamin’s place, so that Benjamin could go home to their father.

study_questions.question: How do we know the brothers had changed?
study_questions.answer: Years before, they sold Joseph and broke their father’s heart. Now they felt sorry for what they’d done, and Judah was willing to give himself up to save Benjamin. God can change anyone’s heart.

fields.title: “I Am Joseph!”
fields.body_html:
“As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.” — Genesis 50:20

When Joseph heard Judah offer to become a slave in place of Benjamin, he couldn’t hold back his tears any longer.

“Everyone leave the room!” he called to his Egyptian servants. When only the brothers were left, Joseph burst into tears. He cried so loudly that the Egyptians outside could hear him.

“I am Joseph!” he said. “Is my father still alive?”

His brothers were too shocked to answer. They were terrified! This powerful man was the brother they had sold as a slave.

“Please, come close to me,” said Joseph. And they came closer. “I am your brother Joseph, the one you sold into Egypt. But don’t be upset, and don’t be angry with yourselves for selling me here. It was to save lives that God sent me ahead of you. There have been two years of famine, and there are still five more to come. God sent me here to keep you alive. So it wasn’t really you who sent me here. It was God.”

Then Joseph hugged his little brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept too. And he kissed all his brothers and cried over them. After that, at last, his brothers could talk to him.

“Hurry home to my father,” said Joseph. “Tell him, ‘God has made your son Joseph ruler of all Egypt. Come down to me. Come and live near me, you and your children and grandchildren and all your animals. I will take care of you.’”

When the brothers got home and told Jacob, he couldn’t believe it at first. But when he saw the carts Joseph had sent to carry him, he said, “My son Joseph is still alive! I will go and see him before I die.”

So Jacob and his whole family moved to Egypt. When Joseph saw his father, he threw his arms around him and wept for a long time. Joseph gave them good land to live in, and food all through the famine.

Many years later, Jacob died. And Joseph’s brothers became afraid again. “What if Joseph still hates us?” they said. “What if he pays us back now for what we did?”

They sent Joseph a message, asking him to forgive them. When Joseph heard it, he cried.

“Don’t be afraid,” Joseph told them. “Am I in the place of God? You meant to do me harm, but God meant it for good, to save the lives of many people. So don’t be afraid. I will take care of you and your children.” And he spoke kindly to them.

Joseph’s brothers did a terrible thing. But God took that terrible thing and turned it into something good. He used it to save Joseph’s whole family, and many other people too. God was in charge all along, keeping His promise to Abraham.

Looking ahead to Jesus: One day Jesus’ enemies would do the most terrible thing of all. They would put Him to death on a cross. But that was part of God’s plan too, and God raised Him from the dead (Acts 2:23–24). God turned the worst thing that ever happened into the best thing that ever happened: the way for us to be forgiven.

Read it in your Bible: Genesis 45; 50:15–21

Dear God, thank you that you can bring good out of bad things. Help me to forgive people who hurt me, the way Joseph forgave his brothers, and the way you forgive me. Amen.

study_questions.question: How did the brothers feel when Joseph told them who he was?
study_questions.answer: They were shocked and terrified, because the brother they had sold as a slave was now the ruler of Egypt.

study_questions.question: What did Joseph say God had done with the bad thing his brothers did?
study_questions.answer: He said, “You meant to do me harm, but God meant it for good.” God used it to save many lives in the famine.

study_questions.question: Joseph forgave his brothers instead of paying them back. Is there someone you need to forgive?
study_questions.answer: Talk about it gently, without pressure. Forgiving doesn’t mean that what happened was all right. It means choosing not to pay someone back, because God has forgiven us. We can ask God for help to do it.
